Ruby Programming Language Cheat Sheet

A practical reference for modern Ruby, aimed at learning Ruby on Debian 13 and building a strong foundation for scripting, automation, and eventually Ruby on Rails.

Version note: This guide targets modern Ruby 4.x conventions. Ruby syntax and standard-library packaging can change between releases. Check ruby -v and the official Ruby documentation when using version-specific features. Most core examples also work on Ruby 3.x unless explicitly noted.

1. Getting Started

Ruby is a dynamic, object-oriented programming language designed to make code expressive and readable. It is commonly used for scripts, automation, web applications, command-line tools, and data processing.

Check the installation

ruby --version
gem --version
bundle --version

On Debian, the distribution package is convenient:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install ruby-full

The Debian package may not be the newest Ruby release. For projects requiring a particular version, a version manager such as rbenv is often more suitable. Avoid mixing system Ruby gems with a separately managed Ruby installation without understanding which executable and gem paths are active.

command -v ruby
command -v gem
ruby -e 'puts RUBY_VERSION'
gem env

Ruby documentation

  • Ruby language and API documentation: https://docs.ruby-lang.org/
  • RubyGems: https://rubygems.org/
  • Bundler: https://bundler.io/

2. Running Ruby

Run a file

# hello.rb
puts "Hello, Ruby!"

ruby hello.rb

Interactive Ruby

irb

At the IRB prompt, try expressions and inspect their return values. Leave with exit or Ctrl-D.

Shebang and executable script

#!/usr/bin/env ruby

puts "Hello from an executable Ruby script"

chmod +x hello.rb
./hello.rb

The shebang uses the ruby found in PATH. Check that this is the Ruby version you intended.

Run a one-liner

ruby -e 'puts RUBY_VERSION'
ruby -e 'ARGV.each { |name| puts "Hello, #{name}" }' Ada Grace

Syntax-check a file

ruby -c script.rb

Useful runtime flags

Command Purpose ———————- ——————————————- ruby file.rb Run a script ruby -e 'CODE' Execute code supplied on the command line ruby -c file.rb Check syntax without running the script ruby -Ilib file.rb Add lib to the load path ruby -w file.rb Enable warnings ruby -v Print Ruby version irb Start the interactive Ruby shell

3. Syntax, Comments, and Output

Ruby uses newlines to separate statements in ordinary code. Semicolons can separate statements, but are rarely needed. Indent consistently, commonly with two spaces.

Comments

# A single-line comment

=begin
A multiline comment.
Use sparingly; ordinary # comments are usually clearer.
=end

Output methods

Method Behavior Typical use ————————- ———————– ———————– puts value Prints value and a Human-readable output newline; arrays are
printed
element-by-element

print value Prints without Prompts and inline automatically adding a output newline

p value Prints an inspect-style Debugging representation and
returns the value

pp value Pretty-prints nested Debugging complex data objects (requires pp)

warn message Writes to standard Warnings error, usually with a
newline

format(template, ...) Returns a formatted Numeric and aligned string output ————————————————————————-

name = "Ada"
puts "Hello, #{name}"
print "Enter your name: "
input = gets
p input
warn "This is a warning"

require "pp"
pp({ user: "Ada", roles: %w[admin editor] })

puts format("Price: $%.2f", 12.5)

puts is usually the right choice for ordinary messages. p is useful when you need to see quotes, nil, or collection structure. Ruby's format/sprintf is useful for controlled formatting; shell-style printf is not the usual Ruby output idiom.

Input

print "What is your name? "
name = gets&.chomp
puts "Hello, #{name || "there"}!"

gets reads a line from standard input. chomp removes the line ending. When input may be absent, account for gets returning nil.

4. Variables, Constants, and Scope

Ruby variables do not need type declarations. The object assigned determines the value's type.

name = "Ada"          # local variable
@name = "Ada"         # instance variable
@@count = 0           # class variable; use cautiously
$debug_mode = false   # global variable; usually avoid
MAX_RETRIES = 3       # constant by convention

Form Meaning ———————————– ———————————– local_name Local variable

@name Instance variable, associated with an object

@@count Class variable shared through a class hierarchy; can be surprising

$global Global variable

CONSTANT Constant; reassignment raises a warning, not a hard immutability guarantee

:symbol Symbol literal, not a variable ———————————————————————–

Multiple assignment

first, second = "Ada", "Grace"
first, second = second, first
head, *tail = [10, 20, 30, 40]

Parallel assignment and return values

def coordinates
  [12, 34]
end

x, y = coordinates

Scope basics

A method has its own local-variable scope. Blocks can access local variables from the surrounding scope, but a class or module body does not behave like a normal method closure.

message = "hello"
3.times { puts message }

def example
  local_inside_method = 1
end
# local_inside_method is not available here

5. Core Data Types

Everything in Ruby is an object, including numbers and nil.

integer = 42
float = 3.14
text = "hello"
symbol = :hello
truth = true
falsehood = false
nothing = nil
array = [1, 2, 3]
hash = { name: "Ada" }

Type Example Notes ———————– ———————– ———————– Integer 42, 1_000_000 Arbitrary-precision integers

Float 3.14 Binary floating-point; not exact for every decimal

Rational Rational(1, 3) Exact rational arithmetic

Complex Complex(1, 2) Complex number

String "hello" Mutable by default

Symbol :name Commonly used for identifiers and hash keys

Array [1, 2, 3] Ordered collection

Hash { name: "Ada" } Key-value collection

Range (1..5) Sequence or interval

Set Set[1, 2, 3] Unique elements; requires set

Boolean true, false The only falsey values are false and nil

NilClass nil Represents absence of a value ———————————————————————–

Inspect an object's class:

42.class       # Integer
"hello".class  # String
nil.class      # NilClass

6. Type Conversion

Conversion methods can differ in strictness. Use strict constructors when invalid input should be rejected.

"42".to_i       # 42
"3.14".to_f     # 3.14
42.to_s         # "42"
"active".to_sym # :active

Integer("42")   # 42
Float("3.14")   # 3.14
Integer("nope") # raises ArgumentError

Be careful: "12cats".to_i returns 12, while Integer("12cats") raises an error. For user input, strict conversion is often safer.

print "Enter an integer: "
raw = gets&.chomp

begin
  number = Integer(raw, 10)
  puts "Twice the value is #{number * 2}"
rescue ArgumentError, TypeError
  warn "Please enter a valid integer."
  exit 1
end

7. Operators

Arithmetic

Operator Meaning Example ———- —————————— ——————— + Addition or concatenation 2 + 3 - Subtraction 5 - 2 * Multiplication or repetition 3 * 4, "ha" * 3 / Division 7 / 2 # => 3 % Remainder 7 % 2 # => 1 ** Exponentiation 2 ** 3 # => 8

Integer divided by integer produces an integer. Use 7.0 / 2, Rational(7, 2), or explicit conversion when appropriate.

Comparison and logical operators

a == b       # value equality
a != b
a < b
a <= b
a <=> b      # -1, 0, 1, or nil
!condition
left && right
left || right

&& and || short-circuit and return one of their operands, not necessarily true or false.

Other useful operators

Operator Meaning ———————— —————————————– = Assignment +=, -=, *=, /= Modify and reassign ||= Assign only if current value is falsey &&= Assign only if current value is truthy .. Inclusive range ... Exclusive upper bound in a range &. Safe navigation :: Constant or namespace resolution ? : Ternary conditional defined? Checks whether an expression is defined

count ||= 0
user_name = user&.name
label = enabled ? "on" : "off"

8. Strings

Quotes and interpolation

single = 'No interpolation: #{2 + 2}'
double = "Interpolation: #{2 + 2}"
escaped = "First line\nSecond line"

Single-quoted strings only process a small set of escapes, primarily \\ and \'. Double-quoted strings support interpolation and common escape sequences.

Common string methods

text = "  Ruby is fun  "

text.strip           # "Ruby is fun"
text.downcase
text.upcase
text.capitalize
text.include?("Ruby")
text.start_with?("  ")
text.end_with?("  ")
text.sub("fun", "useful")       # replace first match
text.gsub(" ", "_")             # replace all matches
text.split
text.length
text.empty?
text.delete(" ")
text.reverse

Indexing and slicing

word = "Ruby"
word[0]       # "R"
word[-1]      # "y"
word[0, 2]    # "Ru"
word[1..2]    # "ub"
word[0] = "T" # mutates word to "Tuby"

Formatting

name = "Ada"
score = 97.25

puts format("%s scored %.1f", name, score)
puts format("%-12s %05d", "ID", 42)

Multiline strings and heredocs

message = <<~TEXT
  This is a multiline string.
  Indentation common to all lines is removed.
TEXT

Mutability and freezing

text = "mutable"
text << " string"

FROZEN_TEXT = "constant value".freeze

A constant binding does not automatically freeze the object. Freezing is shallow unless nested objects are frozen separately.

9. Numbers and Math

-7.abs             # 7
3.14159.round(2)   # 3.14
3.9.floor          # 3
3.1.ceil           # 4
(-7).div(3)        # -3, floor division
(-7).remainder(3)  # -1
7.fdiv(2)          # 3.5
Math.sqrt(81)      # 9.0
Math.log(Math::E)  # 1.0

Use Random for random values:

rng = Random.new
rng.rand(1..6)       # 1 through 6
rng.rand             # float in [0.0, 1.0)

Do not use ordinary pseudorandom numbers for security tokens. Use SecureRandom:

require "securerandom"
token = SecureRandom.hex(32)

For financial calculations, understand floating-point rounding. Consider integer minor units (such as cents) or BigDecimal where decimal arithmetic is required.

require "bigdecimal"
price = BigDecimal("19.99")
tax = price * BigDecimal("0.08")

10. Symbols

Symbols are commonly used as identifiers and hash keys.

:active
:"needs review"
:"user-name"

status = :active
status == :active

Symbols and strings are different types:

"name" == :name       # false
"name".to_sym == :name # true

Use symbols for known, internal identifiers. Do not blindly convert arbitrary untrusted input into symbols when working with old Ruby versions or APIs with different symbol-lifetime behavior. Modern Ruby manages dynamic symbols more safely than older releases, but validation is still good design.

11. Ranges

(1..5).to_a   # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
(1...5).to_a  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
("a".."d").to_a
(1..10).include?(7)

.. includes the end; ... excludes the end.

case score
when 0...60 then "Fail"
when 60...80 then "Pass"
when 80..100 then "Excellent"
else "Out of range"
end

For numeric ranges, cover? checks interval membership efficiently:

(1..1_000_000).cover?(500_000) # true

12. Truthiness and nil

Only false and nil are falsey. Values such as 0, "", and [] are truthy.

if 0
  puts "This runs"
end

if ""
  puts "This also runs"
end

Common checks:

value.nil?
value == false
value.empty?       # only when supported by the value
value.nil? || value.empty?

Avoid using value || default when false is a meaningful value; || falls back for both nil and false.

enabled = settings.fetch(:enabled, true) # preserves explicit false

13. Conditionals

if, elsif, else

if temperature > 30
  puts "Hot"
elsif temperature > 20
  puts "Warm"
else
  puts "Cool"
end

unless

unless logged_in
  puts "Please sign in"
end

Use unless for simple negative conditions. Avoid complicated unless ... else expressions.

Modifier forms

puts "Ready" if ready
warn "Missing configuration" unless configured

case

case command
when "start"
  puts "Starting"
when "stop", "quit"
  puts "Stopping"
else
  warn "Unknown command"
end

Ternary operator

message = valid ? "Accepted" : "Rejected"

Prefer a normal if expression when the branches are long or nested.

14. Pattern Matching

Ruby pattern matching uses case with in. It is different from a regular-expression match.

case [200, "OK"]
in [200, message]
  puts "Success: #{message}"
in [404, message]
  puts "Not found: #{message}"
else
  puts "Other response"
end

Match an array or hash shape

case { name: "Ada", role: "admin" }
in { name:, role: "admin" }
  puts "#{name} is an administrator"
else
  puts "Not an administrator"
end

Guards

case number
in Integer => value if value.positive?
  puts "Positive integer: #{value}"
else
  puts "Something else"
end

Pattern matching is useful for structured data, but ordinary if and case/when are often simpler for basic conditions. Syntax and refinements to pattern matching vary by Ruby version; test against your project's target version.

15. Loops and Iteration

Ruby often favors collection iterators over manual loops.

each

%w[red green blue].each do |color|
  puts color
end

times, upto, and downto

3.times { |index| puts index }
1.upto(3) { |number| puts number }
3.downto(1) { |number| puts number }

while and until

count = 0
while count < 3
  puts count
  count += 1
end

until count == 0
  count -= 1
end

loop, break, next, and redo

loop do
  input = gets&.chomp
  break if input.nil? || input == "quit"
  next if input.empty?

  puts "You entered: #{input}"
end
  • break: exit the loop.
  • next: skip to the next iteration.
  • redo: repeat the current iteration without rechecking the loop condition. Use carefully to avoid infinite loops.

for

for item in %w[one two three]
  puts item
end

for is valid Ruby, but each is more idiomatic and has different variable-scope behavior.

16. Blocks, Procs, and Lambdas

A block is a chunk of code passed to a method.

[1, 2, 3].each { |number| puts number }

[1, 2, 3].each do |number|
  puts number
end

Braces are common for short, single-expression blocks. do...end is often clearer for multiline blocks.

Yield to a block

def around
  puts "Before"
  yield if block_given?
  puts "After"
end

around { puts "Inside" }

Capture a block

def run_twice(&block)
  2.times { block.call }
end

run_twice { puts "Hello" }

Proc and lambda

greeter = Proc.new { |name| puts "Hello, #{name}" }
greeter.call("Ada")

strict_greeter = ->(name) { puts "Hello, #{name}" }
strict_greeter.call("Grace")

Lambdas enforce argument arity more strictly and handle return differently from ordinary procs. Use ->(...) { ... } for a lambda literal.

17. Arrays

Create and access

numbers = [10, 20, 30]
words = %w[ruby bash python]
symbols = %i[read write execute]

numbers[0]      # 10
numbers[-1]     # 30
numbers.first
numbers.last
numbers[0, 2]   # [10, 20]
numbers[1..]    # [20, 30]

Add and remove

items = ["a", "b"]
items << "c"
items.push("d")
items.unshift("start")
items.pop
items.shift
items.insert(1, "new")
items.delete("b")
items.delete_at(0)

Search, sort, and transform

numbers.include?(20)
numbers.index(30)
numbers.reverse
numbers.sort
numbers.uniq
numbers.compact
numbers.flatten
numbers.join(", ")
numbers.sample

Mutation versus non-mutation

Many mutating methods end in ! by convention, but not every method ending in ! simply means "mutates." Read the method documentation.

names = %w[ada grace]
upper = names.map(&:upcase) # new array
names.map!(&:upcase)        # modifies names

Array pitfalls

Array.new(3, [])       # all positions reference the SAME inner array
Array.new(3) { [] }    # each position gets a different array

18. Hashes

Hashes store key-value pairs.

person = { name: "Ada", age: 36 }
person[:name]
person.fetch(:age)
person.fetch(:email, "not provided")
person.key?(:name)
person.value?("Ada")

Add, update, and remove

person[:role] = "engineer"
person.merge!(active: true)
person.delete(:age)
person.keys
person.values
person.length

Iterate

person.each do |key, value|
  puts "#{key}: #{value}"
end

Default values

counts = Hash.new(0)
counts["ruby"] += 1

groups = Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] }
groups["languages"] << "Ruby"

Be cautious with mutable shared defaults:

bad = Hash.new([]) # the same array is returned for missing keys
good = Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] }

Keyword-style hashes

options = { timeout: 5, retries: 2 }

A hash with symbol keys is common in Ruby, but external JSON data generally uses string keys.

19. Enumerable and Collection Processing

Enumerable provides powerful methods to classes that implement each.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

numbers.map { |n| n * 2 }          # transform
numbers.select { |n| n.even? }     # keep matching items
numbers.reject { |n| n.even? }     # discard matching items
numbers.find { |n| n > 3 }         # first match
numbers.any?(&:negative?)
numbers.all?(&:positive?)
numbers.none?(&:zero?)
numbers.count(&:odd?)
numbers.sum
numbers.min
numbers.max
numbers.partition(&:even?)
numbers.group_by(&:even?)

reduce / inject

[1, 2, 3, 4].reduce(0) { |sum, n| sum + n }
[1, 2, 3, 4].reduce(:+)

For simple sums, use sum. Use reduce when building a value that requires custom accumulation.

filter_map

["12", "bad", "7"].filter_map do |text|
  Integer(text, exception: false)
end
# => [12, 7]

Method references with &:

%w[ruby rails].map(&:upcase)

This shorthand passes a method as a block. Use an explicit block when the operation needs arguments or extra logic.

Chaining

results = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
  .select(&:even?)
  .map { |n| n * n }
  .sum

Keep pipelines readable. For very large data, avoid building unnecessary intermediate arrays.

20. Sets, Destructuring, and Enumerators

Sets

require "set"

a = Set[1, 2, 3]
b = Set[3, 4, 5]

a | b  # union
a & b  # intersection
a - b  # difference
a.add(4)
a.include?(2)

Splat and double-splat

def show(first, *rest)
  p first
  p rest
end

show("a", "b", "c")

def configure(**options)
  p options
end

configure(timeout: 5, retries: 3)
  • * expands or captures positional arguments.
  • ** expands or captures keyword arguments / hash-like options.
  • & converts between a block and a Proc in method calls.

Destructuring

first, second = [10, 20]
name, *roles = ["Ada", "admin", "editor"]

Enumerators and lazy evaluation

enum = [1, 2, 3].each
enum.next # 1
enum.next # 2

result = (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy
  .select(&:even?)
  .first(5)
# => [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

Lazy enumerators can avoid calculating every intermediate value. They are especially useful for large or potentially infinite sequences.

21. Methods

Define a method

def greet(name)
  "Hello, #{name}!"
end

puts greet("Ada")

Ruby returns the last evaluated expression unless return is used.

Default and keyword arguments

def connect(host, port = 443, secure: true, timeout: 5)
  { host: host, port: port, secure: secure, timeout: timeout }
end

connect("example.com")
connect("example.com", 8443, secure: false)

Argument forwarding and validation

def divide(a, b)
  raise ArgumentError, "divisor cannot be zero" if b.zero?
  a.to_f / b
end

Predicate, bang, and setter conventions

valid?
normalize!
name=
  • ? commonly marks a predicate.
  • ! often signals a more dangerous or mutating variant, but is only a naming convention.
  • = at the end marks a setter method.

Visibility

class Account
  def balance
    @balance
  end

  private

  def recalculate
    # internal implementation
  end
end

22. Object-Oriented Programming

Class and instance

class User
  attr_reader :name

  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end

  def greet
    "Hello, #{@name}"
  end
end

user = User.new("Ada")
puts user.greet

initialize runs during object construction. attr_reader, attr_writer, and attr_accessor define accessors.

Instance and class methods

class Counter
  @@instances = 0 # class variables can have surprising inheritance behavior

  def initialize
    @count = 0
    @@instances += 1
  end

  def increment
    @count += 1
  end

  def self.instances
    @@instances
  end
end

Prefer a class-instance variable or another explicit design over class variables when inheritance behavior could confuse readers.

class Registry
  @items = []

  class << self
    attr_reader :items
  end
end

Inheritance and super

class Animal
  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end

  def speak
    "#{@name} makes a sound"
  end
end

class Dog < Animal
  def speak
    "#{super} and barks"
  end
end

Composition

Composition means an object uses another object rather than inheriting all its behavior.

class Report
  def initialize(formatter)
    @formatter = formatter
  end

  def render(data)
    @formatter.call(data)
  end
end

Duck typing

Ruby code often depends on what an object can do rather than its exact class.

def print_lines(source)
  source.each_line { |line| puts line }
end

Any object implementing the needed interface can be passed. This is flexible, but document expectations and validate inputs when necessary.

23. Modules, Mixins, and Namespaces

Namespace

module MyApp
  VERSION = "1.0.0"

  class User
  end
end

user = MyApp::User.new

Mixin with include

module Timestamped
  def timestamp
    Time.now
  end
end

class Event
  include Timestamped
end

extend and prepend

  • include: adds module instance methods to the class's instances.
  • extend: adds module methods to a particular object, often class methods.
  • prepend: places a module before a class in method lookup, often used to wrap behavior.
module ClassHelpers
  def category
    "example"
  end
end

class Product
  extend ClassHelpers
end

Product.category

Modules are also useful for constants and avoiding name collisions. Prefer small, cohesive modules over large collections of unrelated methods.

24. Introspection and Metaprogramming

Ruby can inspect objects at runtime.

value = "hello"

value.class
value.is_a?(String)
value.respond_to?(:upcase)
value.methods.include?(:upcase)
value.instance_variables

Dynamic method invocation

"hello".public_send(:upcase)

Prefer public_send when calling a method by name supplied at runtime because it respects public visibility. Do not pass untrusted method names without an allowlist.

Define a method dynamically

class Greeter
  define_method(:greet) do |name|
    "Hello, #{name}"
  end
end

Metaprogramming can reduce repetition but can also make code harder to debug, search, and refactor. Use ordinary methods unless dynamic behavior provides a clear benefit.

Avoid using eval to execute strings assembled from user input.

25. Files and Directories

Read and write

text = File.read("input.txt", encoding: "UTF-8")
File.write("output.txt", "Hello\n")
File.write("output.txt", "More text\n", mode: "a")

Safe resource handling

File.open("input.txt", "r") do |file|
  file.each_line do |line|
    puts line.chomp
  end
end

The block form closes the file even if an exception occurs.

Process a large file line by line

File.foreach("large.log") do |line|
  next unless line.include?("ERROR")
  puts line
end

Avoid File.read for very large files if you do not need the entire contents in memory.

Paths

path = File.join("data", "report.csv")
File.expand_path(path)
File.basename(path)
File.dirname(path)
File.extname(path)
File.exist?(path)
File.file?(path)
File.directory?(path)
File.size(path) if File.file?(path)

Use File.join instead of manually assembling paths with /. File.expand_path normalizes a path but does not prove that it is safe or authorized.

Directories and globbing

Dir.pwd
Dir.entries(".")
Dir.glob("logs/*.log").each { |path| puts path }
Dir.mkdir("output") unless Dir.exist?("output")

Temporary files

require "tempfile"

Tempfile.create("report") do |file|
  file.write("temporary data\n")
  file.flush
  puts file.path
end

The block form manages cleanup. Use temporary files for intermediate data that should not persist.

File permissions and metadata

File.readable?("input.txt")
File.writable?("output.txt")
File.executable?("script.sh")
File.mtime("input.txt")
File.stat("input.txt").mode

Do not assume a file's permissions alone make it safe to read or execute. Consider ownership, symlinks, race conditions, and the directory in which the file lives.

26. Environment, Arguments, and CLI Options

Environment variables

home = ENV["HOME"]
environment = ENV.fetch("APP_ENV", "development")

ENV.fetch is useful for required configuration:

api_key = ENV.fetch("API_KEY") # raises KeyError if missing

Never commit secrets to source control or print them to logs.

Arguments

p ARGV
filename = ARGV.fetch(0, "input.txt")

OptionParser

require "optparse"

options = { verbose: false, limit: 10 }

OptionParser.new do |parser|
  parser.banner = "Usage: ruby report.rb [options]"

  parser.on("-v", "--verbose", "Show details") do
    options[:verbose] = true
  end

  parser.on("-n N", "--limit N", Integer, "Maximum rows") do |n|
    options[:limit] = n
  end

  parser.on("-h", "--help", "Show help") do
    puts parser
    exit
  end
end.parse!

p options
p ARGV

Use OptionParser rather than manually parsing complicated command-line flags.

Standard streams and exit codes

puts "Normal output"       # stdout
warn "Something happened" # stderr
exit 0                     # success
exit 1                     # failure

Conventionally, exit status 0 means success; a nonzero value means failure.

27. Processes and External Commands

External commands are powerful, but unsafe command construction can lead to command injection.

Prefer argument arrays

require "open3"

stdout, stderr, status = Open3.capture3(
  "grep", "-n", "--", "ERROR", "application.log"
)

puts stdout
warn stderr unless stderr.empty?
warn "grep exited with #{status.exitstatus}" unless status.success?

Passing an executable and separate arguments avoids shell parsing. Confirm the executable and its options are appropriate for the platform.

system

success = system("git", "status", "--short")
warn "Git command failed" unless success

system returns true, false, or nil depending on process outcome and whether execution could be started. Inspect $? or use Process::Status when you need the exact exit status.

spawn and exec

  • spawn: starts a child process and returns its PID.
  • exec: replaces the current process with another program.
  • Backticks and %x{}: capture output, but use only with trusted command strings.
  • Open3: captures output, error output, and process status.
pid = spawn("sleep", "1")
Process.wait(pid)

Avoid shell interpolation

Unsafe:

# Do not build a shell command from untrusted input.
system("grep #{user_pattern} #{filename}")

Safer:

system("grep", "-F", "--", user_pattern, filename)

Even with argument arrays, validate paths and options for the specific command. Never assume untrusted data is safe simply because it is passed as an argument.

28. Exceptions and Error Handling

Basic exception handling

begin
  number = Integer("not a number")
rescue ArgumentError => error
  warn "Invalid number: #{error.message}"
ensure
  # Runs whether or not an exception occurred
end

else

begin
  result = Integer("42")
rescue ArgumentError
  warn "Conversion failed"
else
  puts "Converted successfully: #{result}"
ensure
  # Cleanup, if needed
end

else runs only if the begin body finishes without an exception.

Raise an exception

raise ArgumentError, "name cannot be blank" if name.to_s.strip.empty?

Custom exception

class ConfigurationError < StandardError
end

raise ConfigurationError, "Missing APP_ENV"

Best practices

  • Rescue the specific exception you can handle.
  • Avoid rescue Exception; it also catches system-level exceptions that usually should not be swallowed.
  • Do not silently ignore failures.
  • Use ensure for cleanup.
  • Provide actionable error messages without exposing secrets.
  • For expected invalid input, return a clear error or exit with a nonzero status.

29. Regular Expressions and Text Processing

Ruby regular expressions are commonly written as /pattern/.

"ruby 4".match?(/\Aruby/)
"abc123".match?(/\d+/)

Anchors and character classes

Pattern Meaning ————— —————————————– \A Start of string \z End of string ^, $ Line anchors under relevant modes \d Digit \w Word character \s Whitespace . Any character except newline by default [A-Z] Character class +, *, ? Quantifiers {2,5} Repetition range (...) Capture group (?:...) Non-capturing group | Alternation

Match and capture

match = "user-42".match(/\Auser-(\d+)\z/)
if match
  puts match[1]       # "42"
end

Replace

"one two".sub(/\s+/, "-")   # first match
"one two".gsub(/\s+/, "-")  # all matches

Escape untrusted literal text

literal = "a+b"
pattern = Regexp.new(Regexp.escape(literal))

Do not treat arbitrary user input as a regular expression unless that is explicitly intended. Complex regexes can also be vulnerable to excessive backtracking.

30. CSV, JSON, YAML, and XML

Use parsers for structured formats rather than trying to parse them with regular expressions.

CSV

require "csv"

CSV.foreach("people.csv", headers: true) do |row|
  puts row["name"]
end

CSV.open("report.csv", "w", write_headers: true,
         headers: %w[name score]) do |csv|
  csv << ["Ada", 98]
  csv << ["Grace", 95]
end

CSV fields can contain commas, quotes, and newlines. Use the csv library instead of splitting each line on commas.

JSON

require "json"

data = { name: "Ada", roles: %w[admin editor] }
json_text = JSON.generate(data)
puts json_text

parsed = JSON.parse(json_text)
puts parsed["name"]

Parsed JSON object keys are strings by default. Handle malformed input:

begin
  data = JSON.parse(File.read("data.json"))
rescue JSON::ParserError => error
  warn "Invalid JSON: #{error.message}"
  exit 1
end

YAML

require "yaml"

config = YAML.safe_load(
  File.read("config.yml"),
  permitted_classes: [],
  permitted_symbols: [],
  aliases: false
)

YAML loading options vary by Ruby/Psych version. Treat configuration as untrusted unless its source is trusted, and avoid unsafe object deserialization. If aliases are needed, enable them deliberately after assessing the input.

XML and HTML

Use a real parser for general XML or HTML, such as Nokogiri (an external gem). HTML is not reliably parsed with regex alone.

31. Dates, Times, and Encodings

Dates and times

require "date"

today = Date.today
now = Time.now
date = Date.parse("2026-10-24")
time = Time.parse("2026-10-24 14:30:00")

Use Time for timestamps and Date for calendar dates. Be explicit about time zones in distributed applications; a server's local time zone may differ from a user's.

Formatting

now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
Date.today.strftime("%A, %B %-d, %Y")

Common directives: %Y year, %m month, %d day, %H hour (24-hour), %M minute, %S second, %A weekday.

Encoding

text = File.read("input.txt", encoding: "UTF-8")
text.encoding
text.valid_encoding?
text.encode("UTF-8")

An encoding declaration or conversion does not automatically repair arbitrary invalid data. Detect and handle invalid byte sequences deliberately.

32. Networking and HTTP

Basic HTTP GET

require "net/http"
require "uri"
require "json"

uri = URI("https://example.com/api/status")
response = Net::HTTP.start(
  uri.host,
  uri.port,
  use_ssl: uri.scheme == "https",
  open_timeout: 5,
  read_timeout: 10
) do |http|
  http.get(uri.request_uri)
end

if response.is_a?(Net::HTTPSuccess)
  puts response.body
else
  warn "HTTP request failed: #{response.code}"
end

For a real API client, also consider write timeouts, redirects, response-size limits, content types, rate limits, retries, and JSON parsing errors. Verify TLS certificates; do not disable TLS verification to work around certificate errors.

POST JSON

require "net/http"
require "uri"
require "json"

uri = URI("https://example.com/api/items")
request = Net::HTTP::Post.new(uri)
request["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
request["Accept"] = "application/json"
request.body = JSON.generate(name: "sample")

response = Net::HTTP.start(
  uri.host,
  uri.port,
  use_ssl: uri.scheme == "https",
  open_timeout: 5,
  read_timeout: 10
) do |http|
  http.request(request)
end

puts response.code

Use placeholder domains in examples and replace them with a real, documented API endpoint when experimenting. Never hard-code API keys into source code.

33. Loading Code, Gems, and Bundler

require and load

require "json"         # loads a feature once
require "set"
load "./development.rb" # loads file again each time called

Prefer require for libraries. load is mainly useful when intentionally reloading a file.

Install and inspect gems

gem list
gem info json
gem install rake
gem uninstall rake

Avoid using sudo gem install with a user-managed Ruby unless the installation is deliberately configured for system-wide use.

Bundler

A Gemfile declares project dependencies:

source "https://rubygems.org"

gem "rake"

Common commands:

bundle install
bundle exec ruby script.rb
bundle exec rake
bundle update rake
bundle check

Commit Gemfile.lock for applications and executable projects so dependency resolution is repeatable. Update dependencies deliberately and test the result.

Standard library versus external gem

Many useful libraries ship with Ruby or are distributed with the Ruby installation, but packaging can vary by version and distribution. If require "csv" or another library fails, check whether its gem/package is installed for the active Ruby version. Do not assume every library is bundled identically across Ruby 3.x and 4.x.

34. Project Structure and Rake

A small project might look like:

my_tool/
├── bin/
│   └── my_tool
├── lib/
│   └── my_tool.rb
├── test/
│   └── test_my_tool.rb
├── Gemfile
├── Gemfile.lock
├── Rakefile
└── README.md

Load project code

require_relative "../lib/my_tool"

Use require_relative for files relative to the current source file. Avoid relying on the process's current working directory for locating source files.

Simple Rakefile

require "rake"

desc "Run the test suite"
task :test do
  ruby "-Itest", "test/test_my_tool.rb"
end

Run:

bundle exec rake test

For a real gem, use a standard gem layout and a gemspec. Keep command-line entry points thin and move reusable behavior into lib/.

35. Testing and Debugging

Built-in Minitest

require "minitest/autorun"

def add(a, b)
  a + b
end

class AddTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_adds_two_numbers
    assert_equal 5, add(2, 3)
  end
end

Run the test file:

ruby test_add.rb

Useful assertions include assert, refute, assert_equal, assert_nil, assert_raises, and assert_includes.

Debugging

p variable
pp complex_object
warn "Reached checkpoint"

Modern Ruby supports interactive debugging with the debug library when available:

require "debug"
binding.break

Debugging tools and commands can vary by Ruby version and installed packages. Remove temporary debug statements before committing code.

Testing principles

  • Test normal inputs, edge cases, and invalid inputs.
  • Keep tests repeatable and independent.
  • Avoid relying on real external services in unit tests.
  • Use temporary directories and files for filesystem tests.
  • Test error behavior as well as successful results.

36. Logging and Performance

Logger

require "logger"

logger = Logger.new($stderr)
logger.level = Logger::INFO

logger.debug("Detailed diagnostic information")
logger.info("Job started")
logger.warn("Configuration is incomplete")
logger.error("Job failed")

Never log passwords, API tokens, private keys, or sensitive user data. Add context that helps diagnose a problem without exposing secrets.

Benchmark

require "benchmark"

Benchmark.bm do |benchmark|
  benchmark.report("sum:") { 1_000_000.times.sum { |n| n } }
end

Benchmark representative work rather than tiny examples alone. For real performance issues, profile first and optimize the measured bottleneck.

Complexity reminders

Operation Typical complexity ————————— ——————– Array indexing O(1) Array search O(n) Hash lookup Average O(1) Set membership Average O(1) Sorting Usually O(n log n) Full collection traversal O(n)

Actual costs depend on the data structure, implementation, and operation.

37. Concurrency Overview

Ruby provides several ways to perform work concurrently:

  • Threads: useful for overlapping I/O; MRI's Global VM Lock affects parallel execution of Ruby code.
  • Processes: separate address spaces; useful for CPU-bound work or isolation.
  • Fibers: lightweight cooperative execution units; useful with fiber-aware I/O and schedulers.
  • Queue: a thread-safe communication primitive for producer-consumer patterns.
require "thread"

queue = Queue.new
worker = Thread.new do
  queue << "done"
end

puts queue.pop
worker.join

Concurrency behavior depends on the Ruby implementation and libraries. Do not assume threads automatically make CPU-bound Ruby code run in parallel. Protect shared mutable state and understand the lifecycle of worker threads.

38. Modern Ruby Features and Compatibility

Ruby evolves over time. Check the project's target version before using newer syntax.

Feature Notes ———————————– ———————————– Keyword arguments Modern, explicit argument style; details changed in Ruby 3.0

Safe navigation &. Avoids calling a method on nil; available since Ruby 2.3

Pattern matching case/in Introduced in Ruby 2.7 and refined in later releases

Endless method definitions def name = expression; introduced in Ruby 3.0

Numbered block parameters _1, Convenient for simple blocks; _2 available in modern Ruby

Data.define Immutable value-object facility introduced in Ruby 3.2

filter_map Transform and discard nil/false results; available since Ruby 2.7

Hash#transform_keys / Useful hash transformations; verify transform_values older target versions

... argument forwarding For forwarding arguments, introduced in Ruby 2.7

it block parameter Availability and semantics are version-specific; verify before using ———————————————————————–

Examples:

# Safe navigation
user&.profile&.name

# Endless method
def double(number) = number * 2

# Numbered block parameter
[1, 2, 3].map { _1 * 2 }

# Data class for a small immutable value object (Ruby 3.2+)
Point = Data.define(:x, :y)
point = Point.new(x: 2, y: 5)

Use the newest syntax when your project controls its Ruby version. For reusable libraries, consider the minimum supported Ruby version and test against it.

39. Security and Best Practices

Input validation

Treat command-line input, environment variables, files, API responses, and user-submitted values as untrusted until validated.

port = Integer(ENV.fetch("PORT", "3000"), 10)
raise ArgumentError, "port out of range" unless (1..65_535).cover?(port)

Avoid unsafe evaluation

Do not use eval to parse data or execute input. Use purpose-built parsers such as JSON.parse and CSV.

External commands

  • Prefer system("command", "arg1", "arg2") or Open3 with separate arguments.
  • Avoid interpolating untrusted values into shell command strings.
  • Validate paths and command options, even when using argument arrays.
  • Check exit statuses and handle stderr.

Filesystem safety

  • Use File.join for paths.
  • Avoid writing to privileged locations with untrusted filenames.
  • Consider symlinks and race conditions.
  • Use block-based file handling for automatic cleanup.
  • Use temporary directories/files for intermediate artifacts.

Secrets and network security

  • Read secrets from environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager.
  • Do not commit credentials to Git.
  • Keep TLS certificate verification enabled.
  • Set timeouts on network operations.
  • Validate response status, content type, and size.
  • Do not trust remote JSON/YAML just because it is syntactically valid.

Dependencies

  • Keep dependencies minimal.
  • Use Gemfile.lock where appropriate.
  • Review dependency updates and security advisories.
  • Avoid running install commands as root without a clear reason.
  • Prefer supported Ruby releases and update deliberately.

General style

  • Prefer small methods with clear names.
  • Use each, map, select, and other Enumerable methods when they improve readability.
  • Use puts for ordinary output, p for inspection, warn for diagnostics, and format for formatted output.
  • Avoid global variables and unnecessary class variables.
  • Rescue only exceptions you can handle.
  • Prefer composition to deep inheritance.
  • Do not use clever syntax when straightforward code is clearer.

40. Ruby Compared with Bash

Ruby and Bash solve overlapping but different problems. Bash excels at shell orchestration; Ruby is generally more comfortable for structured data, complex logic, and larger reusable programs.

Task Bash Ruby ———————– ———————————————— ——————————————- Print a line printf '%s\n' "$name" puts name

Read a line IFS= read -r name name = gets&.chomp

Variable name="Ada" name = "Ada"

Condition if [[ $x -gt 5 ]]; then ... fi if x > 5 ... end

Iterate files for file in *.log; do ...; done Dir.glob("*.log").each { \|file\| ... }

Read a file while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file File.foreach("file") { \|line\| ... }

JSON External jq is commonly used require "json"

CSV Requires careful parsing or tools require "csv"

HTTP Commonly curl net/http or an HTTP gem

Run a process Shell command system, spawn, or Open3

Data collection Arrays / strings Arrays, hashes, sets, enumerables

Dependencies OS packages and shell utilities RubyGems and Bundler ——————————————————————————————————————–

Ruby's puts is idiomatic for line output. Use printf in Ruby only when formatting control is useful, for example printf("Progress: %3d%%\n", percent).

split Split into an array

match? Check a regular expression without returning a match object

Check type File.join Join path components File.basename / File.dirname Extract path components Dir.glob Match path patterns Dir.pwd Current working directory

Useful standard libraries

Some standard-library components may be packaged separately or as gems depending on the Ruby version and distribution. If require fails, verify the active Ruby installation and package availability.

42. Common Mistakes

Assuming 0 or an empty string is falsey

if 0
  puts "Runs in Ruby"
end

Only false and nil are falsey.

Integer division

7 / 2    # => 3
7.0 / 2  # => 3.5

Using to_i for strict validation

"12cats".to_i     # => 12
Integer("12cats") # raises ArgumentError

Forgetting chomp

name = gets&.chomp

Without chomp, the newline may remain in the string.

Confusing puts, p, and print

  • puts: normal human-readable output.
  • print: output without an automatic newline.
  • p: debug representation.
  • format / printf: controlled formatting.

Assuming a constant makes an object immutable

SETTINGS = { mode: "safe" }
SETTINGS[:mode] = "other" # allowed unless the object is frozen

Accidentally sharing mutable defaults

Use Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] } rather than Hash.new([]) when each key needs its own array.

Catching every exception

Avoid broad rescue clauses that hide programming errors or system-level failures. Catch the expected exception and respond meaningfully.

Building shell commands with interpolation

Do not assemble command strings from untrusted values. Pass the executable and arguments separately.

Parsing CSV or HTML manually

Use dedicated parsers. Commas, quotes, line breaks, and nested markup make ad hoc parsing unreliable.

Assuming every Ruby version has identical libraries

Check the active interpreter, standard-library packaging, and target version before relying on a feature.

43. Learning Path and Mini-Projects

Suggested learning order

  1. Variables, types, strings, operators, and input/output.
  2. Conditionals, loops, arrays, hashes, and methods.
  3. Blocks, Enumerable, and idiomatic collection processing.
  4. Classes, modules, object composition, and exceptions.
  5. Files, directories, command-line arguments, and subprocesses.
  6. CSV/JSON, regular expressions, dates, and HTTP.
  7. Gems, Bundler, project structure, tests, and logging.
  8. Security, performance, concurrency, and advanced Ruby features.

Practice projects

Project Concepts practiced ———————————– ———————————– Unit converter Methods, input, numeric conversion

Number guessing game Conditions, loops, random values

Word and line counter File processing, hashes, CLI arguments

Log analyzer File.foreach, regex, Enumerable, sorting

CSV report generator CSV, data transformation, formatting

JSON configuration checker JSON, validation, exceptions

File organizer Pathname, FileUtils, filesystem safety

System information report External commands, Open3, exit status

HTTP status checker net/http, timeouts, error handling

Command-line task manager Classes, persistence, JSON, OptionParser

Backup verifier File metadata, checksums, logging

Small gem Project layout, tests, Bundler, documentation ———————————————————————–

Final checklist

Before calling a Ruby script finished, ask:

  • Does it validate its inputs?
  • Does it handle expected errors and return a meaningful exit status?
  • Does it avoid unsafe shell interpolation?
  • Does it close files and clean up temporary resources?
  • Does it avoid exposing secrets in output or logs?
  • Are dependencies declared and reproducible?
  • Are important behaviors covered by tests?
  • Does the code use clear, idiomatic Ruby rather than unnecessary cleverness?

Keep this guide nearby, but use it alongside the official documentation. A cheat sheet helps you remember syntax; the API documentation explains edge cases, version-specific behavior, and method contracts.
